sentences.text: Physornis is recognized as one of the largest known terror birds.
Based on comparisons with relatives, this bird may have reached a height of 2 meters at the head.
A preserved lower jaw measured 15 cm in length, while the leg bone known as the tarsometatarsus was stocky with a large, flat top surface.
It was flightless, a trait evidenced by the proportional size of its wings relative to its body mass, with wing size being more reduced in larger group members.
Physornis was scientifically described by Florentino Ameghino in 1895.

The initial discovery consisted of a single fossil fragment comprising the mandibular symphysis and part of the right mandible, found in the Pyrotherium beds near Puerto Deseado in eastern Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
Fossils of this animal have only been found in Deseadan deposits in Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces.

Physornis shares characteristics with graviportal, large-bodied dromornithids and Gastornis. Unlike the running genera Phorusrhacos, Procariama, and Psilopterus, Physornis was a graviportal ambush hunter.
Brazilian researchers Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling discussed phorusrhacid habits in a 2003 article.
The species formerly known as P. brasiliensis is now classified in the genus Paraphysornis.
Alvarenga and Höfling classified Physornis as a close relative of Paraphysornis and Brontornis, noting Brontornis is now a galliform.
Brodkorb and other studies have considered Aucornis eurhynchus a synonym of P. fortis.
Alvarenga and Höfling classified Aucornis solidus as a species inquirenda in 2003 due to potential synonymy with Andrewsornis.
Physornis fossils date from the Oligocene to the Miocene epochs, with a time range from the Rupelian to the Late Pleistocene, approximately 29 to 0.0117 million years ago.
The animal lived during the Oligocene epoch in what is now Argentina, inhabiting South America during this period.

In 1941, Bryan Patterson suggested the holotype might not be avian, speculating it could be a fragment from a giant mammal like Parastrapotherium or Pyrotherium, and provisionally classified the holotype as a nomen dubium.
Pierce Brodkorb argued in 1967 that the holotype was valid.
